wars.name: First Punic War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Carthage evacuates Sicily and pays 3,200 talents; western Sicily becomes Rome's first overseas possession
wars.summary: Twenty-three years of war for Sicily, begun over the Mamertines of Messana, in which Rome built its first battle fleets, won at Mylae, Ecnomus and finally the Aegates, and lost hundreds of ships to Carthaginian skill and Mediterranean storms. Polybius calls it the longest, most continuous and greatest war he knew of.
wars.detail: On land Rome quickly overran most of Sicily but could not take the western fortresses of Lilybaeum and Drepana. At sea, the corvus let Roman marines beat more skilful Carthaginian crews, and Rome invaded Africa in 256, only for Regulus to be destroyed by Xanthippus. Storms in 255, 253 and 249 and the defeat at Drepana cost Rome perhaps 600-700 warships and well over 100,000 men. The war was won by Roman willingness to absorb loss: a final fleet built on private credit destroyed Carthage's last relief attempt in 241. Polybius' account (book 1), based on Fabius Pictor and the pro-Carthaginian Philinus, is the main narrative.

phases.t: Messana and the alliance with Hiero
Agrigentum and the creation of the fleet; Mylae
Storms, Panormus and the siege of Lilybaeum; Drepana
Stalemate: Hamilcar at Heircte and Eryx

scholarship: Lazenby, The First Punic War (1996)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998)
wars.debate: Responsibility for the war (Philinus treaty; Roman aggression versus accident), the true size of the fleets, and the role of the corvus are all debated.

wars.name: Mercenary War (Truceless War)
wars.outcome: Carthaginian victory under Hamilcar Barca; Rome exploits the crisis to seize Sardinia
wars.summary: A savage revolt of Carthage's unpaid mercenaries and Libyan subjects that nearly destroyed Carthage after the First Punic War. Rome stayed formally neutral but seized Sardinia at the end.

phases.t: Mutiny at Sicca and siege of Utica and Hippou Acra
Defeat of Mathos; loss of Sardinia

scholarship: Hoyos, Truceless War (2007)

wars.name: First Illyrian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Teuta pays tribute and is barred from sailing south of Lissus with armed ships; a Roman sphere on the Adriatic coast
wars.summary: Rome's first military intervention across the Adriatic, against Queen Teuta's Ardiaean kingdom after Illyrian piracy and the murder of a Roman envoy.
wars.detail: Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, the Parthini and the Atintani entered Roman fides, and Demetrius of Pharos became a Roman client ruler. Roman envoys explained the war to the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues, Rome's first formal diplomatic contact with mainland Greece.

phases.t: Roman landing and capitulation of Corcyra

scholarship: Hammond, 'Illyris, Rome and Macedon in 229-205 BC', JRS 58 (1968)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)

wars.name: Second Illyrian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Demetrius of Pharos expelled and flees to Philip V
wars.summary: A short campaign by the consuls Aemilius Paullus and Livius Salinator against Demetrius of Pharos, who had broken the 228 treaty, taking Dimale and Pharos.

wars.name: Third Illyrian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; end of the Ardiaean monarchy; Illyria divided into three tributary districts
wars.summary: A thirty-day campaign by the praetor Lucius Anicius Gallus against King Genthius, Perseus' ally, ending with the surrender of Scodra.

wars.name: Gallic War of 225-222
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Boii and Insubres submit; Roman colonies planned on the Po
wars.summary: The great Gallic invasion of Etruria in 225, crushed at Telamon, followed by Roman offensives across the Po culminating in Marcellus' spolia opima at Clastidium and the capture of Mediolanum.
wars.detail: Polybius (2.14-35) gives the war a lengthy excursus, seeing the Gauls as a permanent threat and Rome's victory as the precondition for its resistance to Hannibal. The manpower list of 225 comes from this context.

phases.t: Invasion of Etruria; Faesulae and Telamon
Roman offensives against Boii and Insubres

scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)

wars.name: Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul (200-191)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Boii lose half their land; Cisalpine Gaul south of the Po under Roman control; colonies at Bononia, Parma, Mutina
wars.summary: After Hannibal's departure the Boii and Insubres, encouraged by the Carthaginian officer Hamilcar, renewed the war. Defeats at Cremona (200), the Mincius (197), Comum (196) and Mutina (193) and Nasica's victory over the Boii (191) ended Gallic independence south of the Alps.

phases.t: Mutina and the final defeat of the Boii

scholarship: Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)
Dyson, The Creation of the Roman Frontier (1985)

wars.name: Istrian Wars
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Istria subdued by 177
wars.summary: Two wars against the Istrians at the head of the Adriatic: a campaign against piracy in 221 and the war of 178-177, ended by the capture of Nesactium.

wars.name: Ligurian Wars
wars.outcome: Roman victory after eighty years of intermittent warfare; Apuani deported to Samnium; colonies at Luna and Genua secured
wars.summary: A long, grinding series of mountain wars against the Ligurian tribes of the northern Apennines and Maritime Alps, which Livy calls a training ground for Roman soldiers. Highlights include the deportation of 47,000 Apuani (180) and the scandal of Popillius' enslavement of the Statellates (173).

phases.t: Renewed wars; deportation of the Apuani

scholarship: Dyson, The Creation of the Roman Frontier (1985)

wars.name: Social War (220-217)
wars.outcome: Peace of Naupactus on the basis of the status quo
wars.summary: War of Philip V and the Hellenic Alliance against the Aetolian League, ended at Naupactus in 217 when Philip turned his attention to Italy after Trasimene.
scholarship: Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)

wars.name: Fourth Syrian War
wars.outcome: Ptolemaic victory at Raphia; Coele-Syria remains Ptolemaic
wars.summary: Antiochus III's attempt to conquer Ptolemaic Coele-Syria, ended by Ptolemy IV's victory at Raphia.

wars.name: Fifth Syrian War
wars.outcome: Seleucid victory; Coele-Syria and Judaea pass to Antiochus III
wars.summary: Antiochus III exploited the minority of Ptolemy V to take Coele-Syria, winning at Panium (200); peace was sealed by the marriage of his daughter Cleopatra I to Ptolemy V.

wars.name: Sixth Syrian War
wars.outcome: Antiochus IV forced out of Egypt by Roman ultimatum (Day of Eleusis)
wars.summary: Antiochus IV invaded Egypt twice and was crowned at Memphis, but withdrew when Popillius Laenas delivered the Senate's ultimatum at Eleusis.

wars.name: Second Punic War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Carthage loses Spain and its fleet, pays 10,000 talents over 50 years and may not wage war without Roman permission
wars.summary: The Hannibalic War, the defining conflict of Roman history. Hannibal crossed the Alps and annihilated Roman armies at the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, detaching Capua, much of the south, Syracuse and Macedon from Rome. Rome refused to negotiate, ground down his allies, won the war in Spain under the Scipios, killed Hasdrubal at the Metaurus and finally carried the war to Africa, where Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama.
wars.detail: The war mobilised Roman and allied manpower on an unprecedented scale: some 20-25 legions were in service at the peak (212-211), and perhaps a quarter of Italian adult males served at any time. It produced lasting changes: the denarius, the rise of publicani, extraordinary commands, the devastation of parts of southern Italy (Toynbee's 'Hannibal's Legacy', much debated), Roman involvement in Spain and the Greek East, and the ideology of Roman resilience. Polybius (books 3, 7-15, partly fragmentary) and Livy (books 21-30) are the principal sources; Livy is fuller for Italy but contains annalistic inflation and doublets.

phases.t: War of attrition in Italy; Syracuse, Capua; disaster in Spain
Scipio in Africa; Zama and peace

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)
Hoyos (ed.), A Companion to the Punic Wars (2011)
Toynbee, Hannibal's Legacy (1965)
Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)
Fronda, Between Rome and Carthage (2010)
wars.debate: War guilt (Saguntum, the Ebro treaty, Barcid ambition versus Roman provocation); Hannibal's strategy and why he did not march on Rome after Cannae; the reliability of Livy's figures; the long-term economic effects on Italy (Toynbee versus his critics).

wars.name: First Macedonian War
wars.outcome: Peace of Phoenice: compromise; Philip keeps Atintania, Rome keeps its Illyrian protectorate
wars.summary: A sideshow of the Hannibalic War: Philip V allied with Hannibal and attacked Rome's Illyrian clients; Rome contained him with a fleet and the Aetolian alliance, then made peace at Phoenice.

phases.t: Philip in Illyria; Apollonia; capture of Lissus
Aetolian peace and the Peace of Phoenice

scholarship: Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)

wars.name: Second Macedonian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Philip evacuates Greece, surrenders his fleet, pays 1,000 talents; 'freedom of the Greeks' proclaimed
wars.summary: Launched after appeals from Rhodes and Pergamon and against initial popular reluctance at Rome, the war ended when Flamininus crushed Philip at Cynoscephalae. The settlement proclaimed at the Isthmian Games made Rome the patron of Greek freedom and the arbiter of the Greek world.

phases.t: Flamininus at the Aous; Achaeans join Rome

scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXI-XXXIII (1973)
wars.debate: The key case study in the debate over Roman imperialism: defensive fear (Holleaux), aggressive appetite (Harris), Greek manipulation of Rome (Gruen), or systemic crisis (Eckstein).

wars.name: War against Nabis
wars.outcome: Nabis surrenders Argos and the Laconian coast but keeps Sparta
wars.summary: Flamininus' campaign against Nabis of Sparta to free Argos, the last war of the Greek settlement.

wars.name: Spanish revolt of 197-195
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Cato pacifies the north-east and organises the mines
wars.summary: A general rising in both new Spanish provinces that killed a praetor in 197 and was suppressed by Cato as consul in 195.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

wars.name: Roman-Seleucid War (War of Antiochus)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Treaty of Apamea strips the Seleucids of Asia Minor west of the Taurus and imposes a 15,000-talent indemnity
wars.summary: The confrontation between Rome and Antiochus III, prepared by years of cold war over Thrace and the Greek cities of Asia. Antiochus' small expedition to Greece was routed at Thermopylae (191); naval victories at Corycus, Side and Myonessus let the Scipios cross into Asia, where Magnesia destroyed the Seleucid army.
wars.detail: Rome annexed nothing, enriching Pergamon and Rhodes instead, which created a system of client states and a balance of power under Roman supervision. Hannibal served Antiochus as adviser and admiral.

phases.t: Cold war: Lysimachia and the embassies

scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)
Badian, 'Rome and Antiochus the Great: A Study in Cold War', CPh 54 (1959)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXIV-XXXVII (1981)

wars.name: Aetolian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Aetolians accept a treaty with the maiestas clause and pay 500 talents
wars.summary: Rome's war against its former ally, the Aetolian League, which had invited Antiochus III into Greece: sieges of Heraclea, Naupactus and Ambracia.

wars.name: Galatian War of Manlius Vulso
wars.outcome: Roman victory; the Galatians cease raiding Asia Minor; Eumenes II secure
wars.summary: Manlius Vulso's controversial campaign against the Galatians of central Anatolia after Magnesia, at Mount Olympus and Mount Magaba.

wars.name: First Celtiberian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Gracchan treaties establish a 25-year peace
wars.summary: Campaigns of Fulvius Flaccus and Tiberius Gracchus in the central Meseta, ended by Gracchus' combination of victories and negotiated treaties.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

wars.name: Sardinian War of 177-176
wars.outcome: Roman victory; 80,000 Sardinians killed or enslaved
wars.summary: Tiberius Gracchus' war against the Ilienses and Balari of Sardinia, which flooded the slave markets.

wars.name: Third Macedonian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; end of the Antigonid monarchy; Macedon split into four republics; Epirus sacked
wars.summary: Rome's war against Perseus, prepared by Eumenes' denunciations. After three years of Roman incompetence and Greek sympathy for Perseus, Aemilius Paullus won the war in a single battle at Pydna (168).
wars.detail: The aftermath was harsh: Macedon dismembered, 150,000 Epirotes enslaved, 1,000 Achaeans deported, Rhodes humiliated and ruined, Eumenes snubbed. Polybius (31.25) dates the beginning of Roman moral decline to the wealth and luxury that followed.

phases.t: Pydna; Genthius and the Day of Eleusis
Settlement of Macedonia, sack of Epirus

scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XLI-XLV (2012)

wars.name: Dalmatian War of 156-155
wars.outcome: Roman victory; capture of Delminium
wars.summary: A punitive war against the Dalmatae for attacks on Rome's allies, which Polybius thought the Senate welcomed to keep Italians from softening in peace.

wars.name: Second Celtiberian War
wars.outcome: Peace of Marcellus (152); then Lucullus' unprovoked attack on the Vaccaei
wars.summary: War triggered by Segeda's new walls, marked by Nobilior's defeats (153), Marcellus' negotiated peace (152) and Lucullus' massacre at Cauca (151). The terror it caused led to a levy crisis at Rome.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)

wars.name: Lusitanian War
wars.outcome: Roman victory after the assassination of Viriathus; Lusitanians settled at Valentia; Gallaecia invaded
wars.summary: Two decades of war in the far west of Spain, notorious for Roman perfidy (Galba's massacre of 150, the bribing of Viriathus' murderers in 139) and for the guerrilla genius of Viriathus, who forced a Roman army to capitulate at Erisane (140).

phases.t: Brutus Callaicus in Lusitania and Gallaecia

scholarship: Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)
Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

wars.name: Fourth Macedonian War (revolt of Andriscus)
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Macedonia becomes a Roman province
wars.summary: The rising of the pretender Andriscus, who reunited Macedonia, killed a Roman praetor and was defeated by Metellus at Pydna (148).

wars.name: Third Punic War
wars.outcome: Destruction of Carthage; its territory becomes the province of Africa
wars.summary: Rome's war of annihilation against Carthage, launched on the pretext of Carthage's war against Masinissa. Carthage surrendered its arms, then refused to abandon its city, and held out for three years until Scipio Aemilianus stormed it in 146.

phases.t: Failed assaults by Manilius, Censorinus and Piso
Scipio Aemilianus: blockade, Nepheris, final assault

scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
Ridley, 'To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt', CPh 81 (1986)
wars.debate: Motives: fear of a recovering Carthage (metus Punicus), Cato's influence, greed for land, or the wish to prevent Masinissa from taking Carthage; Polybius 36.9 records Greek debates on the war's justice.

wars.name: Achaean War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Corinth destroyed; Achaean League dissolved; Greece under Roman supervision
wars.summary: The brief, disastrous war of the Achaean League against Rome over Spartan secession, ended by Metellus at Scarpheia and Mummius at Leucopetra and the sack of Corinth.
scholarship: Gruen, 'The Origins of the Achaean War', JHS 96 (1976)
Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
wars.debate: Gruen argued that Rome did not seek the war and that the Achaean leaders miscalculated; Polybius blames the demagogues.

wars.name: Numantine War
wars.outcome: Destruction of Numantia
wars.summary: A decade of humiliation for Rome before the walls of Numantia, a hill town of perhaps 8,000 Arevaci: failed sieges, repudiated treaties (Pompeius 140, Mancinus 137) and the surrender of an army of 20,000, ended only when Scipio Aemilianus encircled the town in 134-133.
scholarship: Schulten, Numantia (1914-1931)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Simon, Roms Kriege in Spanien 154-133 v. Chr. (1962)

wars.name: First Servile War
wars.outcome: Roman victory; Eunus captured; Lex Rupilia reorganises Sicily
wars.summary: The great slave revolt in Sicily under Eunus ('King Antiochus') and Cleon, which defeated several Roman armies before Rupilius took Tauromenium and Enna.
scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
wars.debate: Start date (136, 135 or earlier) and the scale of the revolt (Diodorus' 200,000 is surely inflated).

wars.name: Revolt of Aristonicus
wars.outcome: Roman victory; province of Asia organised by Manius Aquillius (129)
wars.summary: The war that followed Attalus III's bequest: Aristonicus claimed the throne as Eumenes III and raised the poor and slaves of the interior, defeating a consul before his capture in 130/129.
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)
wars.debate: Whether Aristonicus led a social revolution or a dynastic war is debated; the 'Heliopolis' utopia may reflect Stoic ideas (Blossius of Cumae).

campaigns.name: Regulus' invasion of Africa
campaigns.strength: 330 ships at Ecnomus; 15,000 foot and 500 horse left in Africa
campaigns.summary: The first Roman invasion of Africa: the fleet fought its way past the Carthaginian navy at Ecnomus, landed at Aspis, won at Adys and reached Tunes, before Xanthippus destroyed Regulus' army in spring 255.

path.note: embarks the army of both consuls

campaigns.name: The Gallic invasion of 225
campaigns.summary: The Boii, Insubres and Gaesatae crossed the Apennines into Etruria, plundered as far as Clusium, defeated a praetorian army near Faesulae, and, retreating up the coast with their booty, were trapped between two consular armies at Telamon.
campaigns.note: Polybius' topography (Faesulae north, Telamon south) is hard to reconcile; many scholars move the first battle to the Clusium area.

campaigns.name: Hannibal's march to Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse at the Ebro; 38,000 foot and 8,000 horse at the Rhône; 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse on arrival in Italy (Polybius 3.35, 3.56)
campaigns.summary: From New Carthage Hannibal marched across the Ebro and the Pyrenees, forced the Rhône, crossed the Alps in about fifteen days in October-November, took Turin and beat the Romans at the Ticinus and the Trebia.

path.note: subdues the tribes north of the river; leaves Hanno with 10,000

path.t: Through the land of the Volcae

path.note: settles a dispute among the Allobroges
Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis or Traversette

campaigns.note: Alpine pass disputed (Col de la Traversette, Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis, Mont Genèvre, Little St Bernard); the path drawn follows a Clapier route.

campaigns.name: Hannibal's campaigns of 217-216
campaigns.summary: Leaving winter quarters in the Po valley, Hannibal crossed the Apennines and the flooded Arno marshes (losing an eye), destroyed Flaminius at Trasimene, marched to the Adriatic, ravaged Campania under Fabius' eyes, wintered at Gerunium and annihilated the Roman army at Cannae.

path.note: four days and three nights in water; Hannibal loses an eye

path.t: Ravages around Cortona to provoke Flaminius
Ager Falernus and the oxen stratagem

campaigns.name: Hannibal's march on Rome
campaigns.summary: To relieve Capua, Hannibal marched on Rome, camped by the Anio and rode to the Colline Gate, then withdrew, plundering the sanctuary of Feronia, when the besiegers of Capua stayed put. The route given follows Livy (from Coelius); Polybius sends him through Samnium.

path.t: Camp on the Anio; rides to the Colline Gate

campaigns.note: Polybius (9.5-7) and Livy (26.7-11) give different routes.

campaigns.name: Scipio's campaigns in Spain
campaigns.strength: c. 28,000 foot and 3,000 horse at New Carthage (Polybius); 45,000 foot and 3,000 horse at Ilipa
campaigns.summary: Scipio stormed New Carthage, beat Hasdrubal at Baecula and destroyed the last Carthaginian armies at Ilipa, then crossed to Africa to court Syphax and returned to punish rebels and quell a mutiny.

path.note: dines with Hasdrubal son of Gisco at Syphax's table

campaigns.name: Hasdrubal's march to Italy
campaigns.strength: perhaps 30,000 by the Metaurus, with 10 elephants and many Gauls and Ligurians
campaigns.summary: After Baecula Hasdrubal led his army north through Spain, crossed the Pyrenees, wintered among the Arverni, crossed the Alps more easily than his brother and descended into Italy, only to be destroyed at the Metaurus.

path.t: Near Sena Gallica: two consuls face him

campaigns.note: Livy and Appian give few details; the Pyrenean crossing and Alpine pass are unknown.

campaigns.name: Claudius Nero's march to the Metaurus
campaigns.summary: Having intercepted Hasdrubal's letters, Nero slipped away from Hannibal in Apulia with picked troops and marched up the Adriatic coast, about 400 km in six or seven days, fed by the towns along the way, to join Livius Salinator and destroy Hasdrubal.

path.t: Leaves the camp facing Hannibal near Canusium
Joins Livius at Sena Gallica by night
Back facing Hannibal within six days

campaigns.name: Scipio's invasion of Africa
campaigns.strength: c. 25,000-35,000 men from Sicily, later joined by Masinissa's 6,000 foot and 4,000 horse
campaigns.summary: Scipio crossed from Lilybaeum, failed to take Utica, burned the camps of Syphax and Hasdrubal, won the Great Plains, took Tunes and finally defeated Hannibal at Zama.

campaigns.name: Flamininus against Philip V
campaigns.strength: c. 26,000 at Cynoscephalae including Aetolians and 20 elephants
campaigns.summary: Flamininus forced the Aous gorge, marched through Epirus into Thessaly, wintered in Phocis, negotiated at Nicaea, and in 197 brought Philip to battle at Cynoscephalae.

path.t: Peace talks at the Vale of Tempe

campaigns.name: Cato's campaign in Spain
campaigns.summary: Cato sailed from Luna, defeated the Iberians at Emporiae, disarmed the tribes north of the Ebro, marched south to help the praetor in Turdetania, and failed to take Seguntia in Celtiberia before returning to the north-east.

campaigns.name: The Scipios' march to Asia
campaigns.strength: c. 30,000 with Pergamene and Achaean contingents
campaigns.summary: Lucius Scipio, with Africanus as legate, marched overland through Macedonia and Thrace with Philip V's help, crossed the Hellespont unopposed after Myonessus, sacrificed at Ilium and defeated Antiochus at Magnesia.

campaigns.name: Manlius Vulso's Galatian campaign
campaigns.strength: 4 legions and allies with Pergamene troops under Attalus
campaigns.summary: From Ephesus Manlius marched through Caria, Pisidia and Phrygia extorting money from cities and dynasts, then stormed the Galatian refuges on Mount Olympus and Mount Magaba.

path.t: Defeats the Tectosages on Mount Magaba

campaigns.name: Aemilius Paullus' Pydna campaign
campaigns.summary: Paullus crossed to Corcyra, visited Delphi, took over the army facing Perseus on the Elpeus, sent Nasica round by the Pythion pass to turn the Macedonian line, and won at Pydna.

path.t: Takes command on the Elpeus near Dion

campaigns.name: Scipio Aemilianus at Carthage
campaigns.summary: Scipio restored discipline, cut Carthage off from the land with a fortified line across the isthmus, closed the harbour with a mole, destroyed the Punic field army at Nepheris and stormed the city.

path.t: Night assault on the suburb of Megara

campaigns.name: Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia
campaigns.strength: c. 60,000 including allies and Numidians under Jugurtha
campaigns.summary: Scipio drilled the demoralised army, foraged through the land of the Vaccaei to deny Numantia supplies, then built a 9 km circumvallation; the town starved and surrendered in summer 133.

path.t: Takes over the army before Numantia
Forages near Pallantia; ambushed on return

polities.name: Mamertines (Messana)
polities.summary: Campanian ex-mercenaries of Agathocles ('sons of Mars') who seized Messana c. 288; their appeal to Rome and Carthage started the First Punic War, after which they were Roman allies.

polities.name: Libyan and mercenary rebels
polities.summary: Mercenaries and Libyan subjects of Carthage in revolt under Spendius and Mathos during the Truceless War; they struck their own coins inscribed LIBYON.

polities.name: Gaesatae
polities.summary: Gallic warrior bands from the Alps and Rhône valley (the name means 'spearmen' or mercenaries) hired by the Boii and Insubres; fought naked at Telamon and were broken at Clastidium.

polities.name: Istri
polities.summary: People of the Istrian peninsula, accused of piracy; subdued by Rome in 221 and 178-177 (fall of Nesactium).

polities.name: Saguntum
polities.summary: Iberian town (Arse) on the east coast in friendship with Rome; Hannibal's siege of 219 was the casus belli of the Second Punic War. Refounded by Rome after 212.

polities.name: Volcae
polities.summary: Gallic people of Languedoc (Arecomici around Nîmes, Tectosages around Toulouse) who opposed Hannibal's crossing of the Rhône in 218.

polities.name: Taurini
polities.summary: Ligurian-Celtic people of the upper Po whose chief town (Turin) Hannibal stormed in 218.

polities.name: Ilergetes
polities.summary: Iberian people of the lower Segre (Lleida) whose chiefs Indibilis and Mandonius switched between Carthage and Rome and revolted against Scipio in 206-205.

polities.name: Macedonian republics (four merides)
polities.summary: The four autonomous districts into which Rome divided Macedon in 167, with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia, paying tribute to Rome; reunited by Andriscus.

polities.name: Macedon under Andriscus
polities.summary: The short-lived revived Macedonian kingdom of the pretender Andriscus ('Philip VI'), ended by Metellus at Pydna in 148.

polities.name: Kingdom of Eunus (Sicilian slave state)
polities.summary: The rebel slave state of the First Servile War centred on Enna, whose king Eunus took the name Antiochus, held an assembly and minted bronze coins.
